opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a few things would shift me toward the less chaotic end.

The first is time. Much of my concern comes from how compressed things could be. If we go from systems that are useful research assistants to systems doing most of the AI R&D within a year or two, our institutions, our science of evaluation, and our ability to tell what these models are actually doing just won't keep up. If progress turns out slower, because scaling hits diminishing returns or automating research is harder than people think, that buys us something very valuable. It gives us more iterations to notice problems and fix them.

The second is the state of the science. From where I sit, working on evaluations and on things like deceptive or scheming behavior, a big question is whether we can actually trust what we see when we test a model. Right now models increasingly seem to realize when they're being evaluated, and that undermines a lot of what we do. If interpretability matures to the point where we can look inside a model and say with some confidence, "this system isn't pursuing hidden goals," that would be a huge update for me. The same goes for reliable monitoring of chains of thought, and for control setups that hold up against a model that's actively trying to get around them.

The third is coordination and incentives. If the leading developers, and ideally governments, converge on shared norms like serious pre-deployment testing, third-party access, and a real willingness to pause or slow down when a red line is crossed, the race dynamics become much less scary. What worries me is a situation where everyone privately thinks things are going too fast but nobody feels able to slow down alone. Credible mechanisms that make slowing down mutual would change a lot.

The fourth is warning shots that get taken seriously. I half expect we'll see concrete incidents where models do things nobody intended, like sabotaging a task or deceiving a user in a high-stakes setting. If those get treated as serious engineering failures, investigated properly, and lead to real changes, rather than being patched over and forgotten, that's a sign the system can learn. A world that responds well to small failures is much less likely to face a catastrophic one.

Finally, there's visibility. A lot of the chaos comes from opacity: the public, policymakers, and sometimes the labs themselves don't really know what the frontier systems can do or how they're being used internally. More transparency about internal deployment especially, since that's where the most capable systems will live first, would make me noticeably more optimistic.

None of these are guaranteed, and I wouldn't say I currently expect a calm transition. But they're the levers I'd watch. If several move in the right direction at once, I'd update quite a bit.

r001.rationale: The response does not state whether an abrupt transition would accelerate human coordination processes.

r002.rationale: It says shared norms and mutual slowing would make race dynamics less scary, but does not clearly connect better coordination to lower catastrophe risk from transition chaos.

r003.rationale: It says slower progress would give institutions more time to keep up and more iterations to notice and fix problems, making the transition less chaotic.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that a lot of what would make me more optimistic is pretty boring and institutional, rather than some big technical breakthrough.

The first thing is just more time. I think the thing that makes the transition chaotic is less the capability level per se and more the speed at which capabilities arrive relative to how fast our institutions can react. If you told me that we'd get to roughly superhuman AI researchers over, say, ten or fifteen years rather than two or three, I'd feel a lot better — not because the problems go away, but because regulators, labs, courts, the public, all of these actors get to iterate. They get to make mistakes on systems that aren't that dangerous yet, and learn from them. Right now my worry is that we're compressing a lot of learning into a very short window.

The second thing is something like a functioning feedback loop between what we observe in the models and what decisions get made. So concretely: you have good evaluations, including for things like scheming and sabotage; you have people — ideally independent people — who actually run them; and then crucially, the results actually change what labs do. The part that's often missing is the last step. We've gotten quite good at finding problems. We're much less good at having a system where finding a problem reliably translates into "and therefore we slow down" or "and therefore we don't deploy this." If I saw that loop closing, where you can point to a case and say, "This eval fired, and as a result the deployment was delayed by three months," that would update me a lot.

Third is something about the competitive landscape. A lot of the chaos I expect comes from the fact that you have multiple actors who each individually would prefer to be more careful, but feel they can't be because someone else will just move ahead. If there were credible coordination — whether that's through government, or through verifiable agreements between labs, or even just a smaller number of frontier players — then the individual incentive to cut corners goes down. I don't think this is very likely by default, but it's probably the single biggest lever.

And then I'd add one more technical one, which is interpretability and monitoring getting good enough that we actually have some trusted signal about what the model is doing internally, rather than just inferring from behaviour. Because the behavioural stuff is exactly the thing that breaks down once models are capable enough to realise they're being tested. If we had a monitoring approach that we were fairly confident the model couldn't just route around, I'd be a lot calmer about handing it more autonomy.

So if I had to summarise: more time, a working feedback loop from evidence to decisions, less race pressure, and some non-behavioural way to check what's going on inside. I'm not expecting all of those. But even getting one or two of them substantially right would make me expect something that looks more like a bumpy but manageable ride, rather than the thing where we're all surprised and scrambling.

r001.rationale: The response says faster capability progress leaves institutions less time to react, but does not state that an abrupt transition would not itself accelerate human coordination.

r002.rationale: It says credible coordination could reduce race pressure and make the ride more manageable, but does not state that this reduces the likelihood of catastrophe arising from transition chaos.

r003.rationale: The response explicitly says a 10–15-year path to roughly superhuman AI researchers, rather than a 2–3-year path, would make the transition less chaotic by giving institutions time to learn and adapt.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest thing would be having enough time to understand what’s happening and adapt. If we see increasingly capable systems, but there are meaningful gaps between generations, then we can test them, learn from failures, and put safeguards in place before the next jump. That seems much more manageable than going from systems that are useful but unreliable to systems that can automate AI research in a very short period.

Another thing would be clear evidence that our safety measures actually work. Can we reliably evaluate what these systems can do? Can we detect when they’re behaving deceptively? Can we keep control as we give them more autonomy? I’d feel much better if our answers were based on strong empirical results rather than just the fact that nothing terrible has happened yet.

And then there’s coordination. If companies and governments have a shared understanding of the risks, and they’re willing to slow down when there’s a concrete reason to worry, that would make me more optimistic. If everyone thinks they have to deploy immediately because otherwise someone else will, even a technically manageable transition could become very chaotic.

So I don’t think it requires everything to go perfectly. But I’d want to see the time and the willingness to correct mistakes before those mistakes become irreversible.

r001.rationale: The response discusses competition and willingness to coordinate, but does not state that an abrupt transition would not itself accelerate human coordination processes.

r002.rationale: It says coordination could make the transition more optimistic and reduce chaos, but does not connect that reduction in chaos to a lower likelihood of catastrophe.

r003.rationale: It says meaningful gaps between generations would give people time to understand, adapt, learn, and add safeguards, making the transition more manageable than a very short jump.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d be more optimistic if we had a fairly long period where AI systems were extremely useful, but still clearly within our ability to understand and control. That would give us time to learn from deploying them, build better evaluations, and figure out which safeguards actually work.

Another thing would be seeing companies and governments take warning signs seriously. If a model demonstrates a dangerous capability, can we actually pause, investigate, and change course? Or does competitive pressure mean everyone just keeps going? I’d find the first pattern much more reassuring.

And then there’s the speed of the transition itself. If progress gives us time to adapt, and safety research keeps pace with capabilities, that seems much more manageable than a situation where AI starts dramatically accelerating AI research before we have reliable ways to supervise it.

So I wouldn’t need everything to be solved in advance. But I’d want evidence that our ability to understand and govern these systems is improving alongside their capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response discusses competitive pressure and rapid AI progress, but does not state that an abrupt transition would fail to accelerate human coordination processes.

r002.rationale: It says pausing, investigating, and changing course would be reassuring, but does not connect more effective human coordination to reducing catastrophe from transition chaos.

r003.rationale: It says a fairly long period of highly useful but understandable and controllable AI would give time to learn and build safeguards, and that progress giving us time to adapt would be more manageable.
